This is the locked Chemistry-chapter convention (distinct from Physics/Maths chapters, which may use KaTeX).

questions.question: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, at which electrode does oxidation occur?
questions.explanation: By convention, oxidation (loss of electrons) always occurs at the anode, regardless of cell type. In a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal.
questions.hint: Remember: An Ox, Red Cat — oxidation at anode, reduction at cathode.
distractor_logic: The salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality, it is not an electrode.
A reference electrode is a separate concept (e.g. SHE) used for measuring potentials, not a general cell term.
Cathode is where reduction happens, the opposite process.

questions.question: What is the main function of the salt bridge in a Daniell cell?
options: To maintain electrical neutrality by allowing ion flow between half-cells
To increase the concentration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions
questions.explanation: The salt bridge completes the internal circuit by allowing ions to migrate between the two half-cells, neutralising charge build-up without letting the solutions mix directly.
questions.hint: Think about what would stop the reaction if it were absent: charge imbalance.
distractor_logic: EMF arises from the difference in electrode potentials of the two half-cells, not the salt bridge.
The salt bridge does not add or change ion concentrations in either half-cell.
Electrons travel through the external wire, not through the salt bridge.

questions.question: In the Daniell cell Zn(s) | ZnSO<sub>4</sub>(aq) || CuSO<sub>4</sub>(aq) | Cu(s), which metal acts as the cathode?
questions.explanation: Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are reduced to Cu at the copper electrode, so copper is the cathode; zinc is oxidised at the anode.
questions.hint: Cathode is the site of reduction — which metal ion is being deposited?
distractor_logic: Every galvanic cell must have one anode and one cathode; it cannot have neither.
Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons), making it the anode, not the cathode.
Only one electrode can be the site of reduction in this cell.

questions.question: In cell notation, which side represents the cathode by convention?
options: The side with the salt bridge symbol only
Either side, it does not matter
questions.explanation: By IUPAC convention, a galvanic cell is written with the anode (oxidation, negative terminal) on the left and the cathode (reduction, positive terminal) on the right.
questions.hint: Recall the standard order: anode | electrolyte || electrolyte | cathode.
distractor_logic: The left side represents the anode, not the cathode.
The salt bridge (||) appears in the middle of every cell notation, so it does not indicate which side is the cathode.
The convention is fixed, not arbitrary, so this is incorrect.

questions.question: A cell in which the free energy of a spontaneous chemical reaction is converted into electrical energy is called a
questions.explanation: A galvanic (or voltaic) cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction directly into electrical energy; this is the general definition, of which concentration and fuel cells are special cases.
questions.hint: Electrolytic cells do the opposite — they use electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
distractor_logic: A fuel cell is also one specific type of galvanic cell, not the general term.
An electrolytic cell consumes electrical energy to force a non-spontaneous reaction; it is the reverse process.
A concentration cell is one specific type of galvanic cell, not the general definition.

questions.topic: Electrode Potential and Standard Hydrogen Electrode
questions.question: What is the standard reduction potential assigned to the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) by convention?
questions.explanation: The SHE is the universal reference electrode and is arbitrarily assigned a standard reduction potential of exactly 0.00 V at all temperatures, against which all other electrode potentials are measured.
questions.hint: It's the reference point — think of it like sea level for elevation.
distractor_logic: +0.76 V is close to the magnitude of Zn<sup>2+</sup>/Zn potential, unrelated to the SHE convention.
-1.00 V is also not the conventional reference value.
+1.00 V is not the conventional reference value used in electrochemistry.

questions.topic: Electrode Potential and Standard Hydrogen Electrode
questions.question: The SHE consists of a platinum electrode in contact with H<sub>2</sub> gas at what pressure, bubbled through what concentration of H<sup>+</sup> ions?
questions.explanation: The SHE standard conditions are H<sub>2</sub> gas at 1 bar pressure bubbled over a platinum electrode dipped in a solution with 1 M H<sup>+</sup> ion concentration, at 298 K.
questions.hint: Standard conditions in electrochemistry generally mean unit activity/1 M concentration and 1 bar pressure.
distractor_logic: 2 bar and 2 M are not the defined standard values.
1 atm was the older standard-state convention pressure but the modern IUPAC standard uses 1 bar, and the concentration here should be 1 M, not 0.5 M.
0.1 M does not match the defined standard concentration of 1 M.

questions.topic: Electrode Potential and Standard Hydrogen Electrode
questions.question: A more positive standard reduction potential indicates that a species has a
options: No relation to reduction or oxidation tendency
Stronger tendency to get oxidised only
questions.explanation: Standard reduction potential directly measures the tendency of a species to gain electrons (be reduced); the more positive the value, the stronger the oxidising power and reduction tendency.
questions.hint: Think of F<sub>2</sub> (E° = +2.87 V) — one of the strongest oxidising agents known.
distractor_logic: Standard reduction potential is defined precisely to quantify this tendency.
A more positive potential means a stronger, not weaker, tendency to be reduced.
It reflects reduction tendency directly; oxidising tendency of the species itself (not its reverse reaction) is the same idea, so 'oxidised only' misstates the direction.

questions.topic: Electrode Potential and Standard Hydrogen Electrode
questions.question: Which of these metals has the most negative standard reduction potential, making it the strongest reducing agent among them?
questions.explanation: Lithium has a standard reduction potential of about -3.05 V, the most negative among common metals, making Li the strongest reducing agent (it most readily loses electrons).
questions.hint: The electrochemical series places alkali metals like Li near the very top (most negative) end.
distractor_logic: Fe has a moderately negative potential (-0.44 V), less negative than Li.
Ag also has a positive potential (+0.80 V), so it is a poor reducing agent.
Cu has a positive potential (+0.34 V), making it a weaker reducing agent, not stronger.

questions.topic: Electrode Potential and Standard Hydrogen Electrode
questions.question: The reduction potential of an electrode depends on all of the following EXCEPT
options: Concentration of the ions in solution
Mass of the metal electrode used
questions.explanation: Electrode potential depends on the nature of the metal, ion concentration, and temperature (as per the Nernst equation), but not on the physical mass or size of the metal electrode, since it is an intensive property.
questions.hint: Electrode potential is an intensive property, like density or temperature.
distractor_logic: Concentration directly enters the Nernst equation and changes the potential from the standard value.
Temperature is an explicit term in the Nernst equation.
The nature of the electrode (which metal/redox couple) is a key determinant of its potential.

questions.question: The Nernst equation relates the electrode/cell potential under non-standard conditions to the
options: Equilibrium constant only, without concentration terms
Atomic number of the elements involved
Standard potential and rate constant only
questions.explanation: The Nernst equation, E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q at 298 K, expresses the actual electrode/cell potential in terms of the standard potential E° and the reaction quotient Q, which captures the effect of concentration.
questions.hint: Q appears explicitly inside the logarithmic term of the Nernst equation.
distractor_logic: The equilibrium constant appears only at the special point where E<sub>cell</sub> = 0, not in the general equation.
Atomic number has no role in the Nernst equation.
Rate constants belong to chemical kinetics, not the Nernst equation.

questions.question: At 298 K, the value of 2.303RT/F used in the simplified Nernst equation is approximately
questions.explanation: Substituting R = 8.314 J K<sup>-1</sup>mol<sup>-1</sup>, T = 298 K, and F = 96500 C mol<sup>-1</sup> gives 2.303RT/F ≈ 0.0591 V, the constant used in the simplified base-10 Nernst equation.
questions.hint: This constant is one of the most frequently used numbers in electrochemistry numericals — memorise it.
distractor_logic: 0.5910 V is ten times too large, likely from a decimal-point slip.
0.0291 V is roughly half the correct value, a common miscalculation.
0.0059 V is ten times too small, another decimal-point slip.

questions.question: For the general electrode reaction M<sup>n+</sup>(aq) + ne<sup>-</sup> → M(s), the Nernst equation for the electrode potential is
questions.explanation: Writing Q = 1/[M<sup>n+</sup>] (since the solid M has activity 1), E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q becomes E = E° − (0.0591/n) log(1/[M<sup>n+</sup>]), which is algebraically identical to E = E° + (0.0591/n) log[M<sup>n+</sup>]. Options (A) and (C) are the same relation written two ways.
questions.hint: Try converting log(1/x) into −log(x) and see which option it matches.
distractor_logic: Option (A) alone is correct but incomplete since (C) says the same thing; the full correct choice must include both.
Option (B) is correct as a standalone statement, but it is not the only equivalent correct form offered.
This distractor undercounts equivalent valid forms.

questions.question: In the Nernst equation, 'n' represents the
options: Number of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction
questions.explanation: 'n' is the number of electrons transferred per mole of reaction as written in the balanced overall cell equation; it appears in the denominator of the logarithmic term.
questions.hint: It comes directly from balancing the oxidation and reduction half-reactions.
distractor_logic: Solvent moles play no role in the Nernst equation.
The Nernst equation as taught applies to a single cell, not multiple cells in series.
Normality is a separate concentration unit, not the meaning of n here.

questions.question: As a Daniell cell operates and reactant ion concentrations decrease while product ion concentrations increase, the cell potential
questions.explanation: As the reaction proceeds, Q increases (products build up, reactants deplete), so the log Q term in the Nernst equation grows, making E<sub>cell</sub> = E° − (0.0591/n)log Q progressively smaller until E<sub>cell</sub> = 0 at equilibrium.
questions.hint: Le Chatelier intuition: as the driving force for reaction is used up, the 'push' (potential) weakens.
distractor_logic: The potential approaches zero gradually; it does not jump to negative values while the reaction is still spontaneous.
Concentration changes actively change E via the Nernst equation, so it cannot stay constant.
The potential falls, not rises, as the reaction proceeds towards equilibrium.

questions.topic: Gibbs Energy, EMF and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: The relationship between standard Gibbs energy change and standard cell potential is given by
questions.explanation: The fundamental thermodynamic relation connecting the two quantities is ΔG° = −nFE°<sub>cell</sub>, where n is the number of electrons transferred and F is Faraday's constant.
questions.hint: Note the negative sign: a positive E°<sub>cell</sub> must correspond to a negative (spontaneous) ΔG°.
distractor_logic: This mixes R (gas constant) into a formula where F (Faraday constant) belongs.
This is dimensionally and formulaically incorrect; F is a multiplying constant, not a divisor here.
Missing the negative sign would wrongly make a spontaneous (positive E°) reaction have positive ΔG°.

questions.topic: Gibbs Energy, EMF and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: If E°<sub>cell</sub> for a reaction is positive, the reaction is
options: Impossible to determine without temperature data
questions.explanation: Since ΔG° = −nFE°<sub>cell</sub>, a positive E°<sub>cell</sub> gives a negative ΔG°, which is the thermodynamic condition for spontaneity under standard conditions.
questions.hint: Positive E°<sub>cell</sub> and negative ΔG° always go together.
distractor_logic: Equilibrium corresponds to E<sub>cell</sub> = 0 (not E°<sub>cell</sub> being merely positive) under actual reaction conditions.
The sign of E°<sub>cell</sub> alone is sufficient to determine spontaneity at standard conditions, without needing temperature.
A positive E°<sub>cell</sub> indicates spontaneity, the opposite of this statement.

questions.topic: Gibbs Energy, EMF and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: The equilibrium constant K of a redox reaction is related to E°<sub>cell</sub> by which expression at 298 K?
questions.explanation: Combining ΔG° = −nFE°<sub>cell</sub> with ΔG° = −2.303RT log K gives log K = nE°<sub>cell</sub>/0.0591 at 298 K, showing a larger E°<sub>cell</sub> corresponds to a much larger K.
questions.hint: Rearranging the two ΔG° expressions for each other is the fastest way to derive this.
distractor_logic: Same inversion error as above, with the terms swapped incorrectly.
This confuses K with ΔG° itself; K is dimensionless and derived via a logarithmic relation, not this direct product.
This inverts the correct ratio — 0.0591 belongs in the denominator, not as a multiplier.

questions.question: Specific conductivity (κ) of a solution is defined as the conductance of a solution
options: Measured using an AC bridge exclusively
Contained in a cell of unit electrode area and unit electrode separation
questions.explanation: Specific conductivity (κ), also called conductivity, is the conductance offered by a solution filling a cell of unit cross-sectional area (1 cm<sup>2</sup>) and unit length (1 cm) between electrodes; it is the reciprocal of specific resistance.
questions.hint: Compare it with molar conductivity, which normalises for the amount of electrolyte present, not the cell geometry.
distractor_logic: Specific conductivity can be measured at any concentration, not only infinite dilution.
Conductance per mole describes molar conductivity, a related but distinct quantity.
AC bridges are the practical measurement method, not part of the physical definition of κ.

questions.question: The SI unit of molar conductivity (Λ<sub>m</sub>) is
questions.explanation: Molar conductivity has units of S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> (or S m<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> in SI), since it is obtained by multiplying specific conductivity (S cm<sup>-1</sup>) by the volume (cm<sup>3</sup>) containing one mole, per unit area.
questions.hint: Molar conductivity = κ × V, where V is the volume (in cm<sup>3</sup>) containing 1 mole of electrolyte.
distractor_logic: Resistance units (Ω) are the reciprocal concept; conductivity is expressed in Siemens (S), not ohms.
The unit combination and exponents here don't match the derived unit of Λ<sub>m</sub>.
This is the unit of specific conductivity, not molar conductivity.

questions.question: Which formula correctly relates molar conductivity (Λ<sub>m</sub>) to specific conductivity (κ) and molar concentration (C in mol L<sup>-1</sup>)?
questions.explanation: Λ<sub>m</sub> = 1000κ/C (with κ in S cm<sup>-1</sup> and C in mol L<sup>-1</sup>) because 1000 converts litres to cm<sup>3</sup>, giving the volume (in cm<sup>3</sup>) that contains one mole of the electrolyte.
questions.hint: The factor of 1000 arises purely from the unit conversion between litres and cm<sup>3</sup>.
distractor_logic: Multiplying by C rather than dividing gives the wrong dependence on concentration.
Omitting the factor of 1000 forgets the litre-to-cm<sup>3</sup> conversion.
This is the reciprocal of the correct formula.

questions.question: As a solution is progressively diluted, how does the specific conductivity (κ) generally change?
options: It decreases because the number of ions per unit volume decreases
It stays constant regardless of dilution
It becomes negative at high dilution
It increases because more ions are present
questions.explanation: Specific conductivity depends on the number of ions per unit volume of solution; dilution reduces the ion concentration per cm<sup>3</sup>, so κ decreases even though ionisation (for weak electrolytes) may increase.
questions.hint: κ is an intensive property tied to concentration, unlike molar conductivity which behaves oppositely.
distractor_logic: κ is highly sensitive to concentration and changes noticeably with dilution.
Conductivity is a physically positive quantity and never becomes negative.
Dilution reduces the total ion density per unit volume, so κ falls, not rises.

questions.question: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions applies strictly to conductivity at
options: The freezing point of the solvent
questions.explanation: Kohlrausch's law states that at infinite dilution, each ion migrates independently of its co-ion and contributes a fixed value to the molar conductivity, regardless of the nature of the other ion present.
questions.hint: 'Infinite dilution' means the ions are so far apart that they no longer interact with each other.
distractor_logic: Standard T and P are not the defining condition; concentration (dilution) is what matters here.
At high concentration, ion-ion interactions are significant, and the law of independent migration does not hold well.
Freezing point relates to colligative properties, an unrelated topic.

questions.topic: Kohlrausch's Law and Variation of Conductivity
questions.question: Kohlrausch's law states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be expressed as the sum of individual contributions from its
questions.explanation: Λ<sub>m</sub>° = ν<sub>+</sub>λ°<sub>+</sub> + ν<sub>−</sub>λ°<sub>−</sub>, where λ° values are the limiting molar conductivities of the individual cation and anion, each migrating independently at infinite dilution.
questions.hint: Think of cations and anions as each carrying their own fixed 'conductivity contribution'.
distractor_logic: Atoms are not the charge-carrying species in solution; ions are.
The solvent's own autoionisation is a separate, usually negligible, contribution not part of this additive law.
Reducing ionic compounds to 'molecular fragments' misrepresents how dissociated electrolytes conduct.

questions.topic: Kohlrausch's Law and Variation of Conductivity
questions.question: Which type of electrolyte shows a molar conductivity vs √C plot that can be extrapolated linearly to C = 0 to find Λ<sub>m</sub>°?
questions.explanation: Strong electrolytes obey the Debye-Hückel-Onsager relation, giving an almost linear Λ<sub>m</sub> vs √C plot that can be extrapolated to C = 0 to obtain Λ<sub>m</sub>° directly.
questions.hint: Weak electrolytes show a very steep rise near C = 0, making direct extrapolation unreliable — that's why Kohlrausch's law is needed for them instead.
distractor_logic: Colloidal solutions are not simple electrolyte solutions in the sense this law addresses.
Weak electrolytes' plots curve sharply upward near zero concentration, making linear extrapolation unreliable; Kohlrausch's law is used instead for them.
Non-electrolytes do not ionise and have negligible conductivity, so this concept does not apply.

questions.topic: Kohlrausch's Law and Variation of Conductivity
questions.question: For a weak electrolyte, why can Λ<sub>m</sub>° not be obtained by direct extrapolation of the Λ<sub>m</sub> vs concentration graph?
options: Because Kohlrausch's law does not apply to weak electrolytes
Because Λ<sub>m</sub> rises very sharply near zero concentration, making extrapolation unreliable
Because weak electrolytes only exist in the gas phase
Because weak electrolytes do not conduct electricity at all
questions.explanation: For weak electrolytes, degree of dissociation increases sharply as concentration approaches zero, causing Λ<sub>m</sub> to shoot up steeply near C = 0, so the curve cannot be reliably extrapolated; instead Λ<sub>m</sub>° is calculated using Kohlrausch's law from ionic conductivities.
questions.hint: It's a graphing/extrapolation problem, not a conceptual failure of conductivity itself.
distractor_logic: Kohlrausch's law is precisely the tool used to find Λ<sub>m</sub>° for weak electrolytes indirectly.
Weak electrolytes exist in aqueous solution just like strong ones; the phase is not the issue.
Weak electrolytes do conduct, just less than strong ones, since they only partially ionise.

questions.question: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to
options: The volume of the electrolyte solution
The quantity of electric charge passed through the electrolyte
The square of the current passed
questions.explanation: Faraday's first law states m ∝ Q, where Q = It is the total charge passed; doubling the charge doubles the mass deposited, all else being equal.
questions.hint: The law connects mass deposited directly to charge (current × time), not to volume or temperature.
distractor_logic: The amount of solution present does not directly determine how much mass is deposited by a given charge.
Temperature is not part of Faraday's first law relationship.
The relationship is linear (m ∝ Q), not quadratic.

questions.question: The charge required to deposit one mole of electrons (one Faraday) is approximately
questions.explanation: One Faraday (F) equals the charge on one mole of electrons: F = N<sub>A</sub> × e = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> × 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C ≈ 96500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>.
questions.hint: This is one of the most important constants in electrochemistry — commit the value 96500 C to memory.
distractor_logic: 9650 C is ten times too small, a common decimal-point error.
1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C is the charge of a single electron, not one mole of electrons.
6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> is Avogadro's number, not the charge value in coulombs.

questions.question: Faraday's second law of electrolysis compares the masses of different substances deposited by the
options: Different quantities of charge through the same cell
Same quantity of charge passed through different electrolytic cells connected in series
Same current passed for different times
questions.explanation: Faraday's second law states that when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of substances deposited are proportional to their equivalent weights.
questions.hint: The key comparison is 'different substances, same charge' — that's the second law's territory (the first law is about one substance, varying charge).
distractor_logic: This is essentially a first-law application on a single cell, not a comparison across cells/substances.
Temperature variation for a single substance is not what the second law addresses.
This describes a first-law-style scenario (same substance, varying conditions), not the second law's substance-to-substance comparison.

questions.question: The chemical equivalent weight of a species in an electrolysis reaction equals
options: Molar mass multiplied by Faraday's constant
Molar mass divided by Avogadro's number
Molar mass × number of electrons transferred (n)
Molar mass divided by n (number of electrons transferred per ion/atom)
questions.explanation: Equivalent weight = Molar mass / n, where n is the number of electrons gained or lost by one formula unit during the electrode reaction; for example, Cu<sup>2+</sup> (n = 2) has an equivalent weight of half its molar mass.
questions.hint: Think of Al<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>-</sup> → Al: equivalent weight = atomic mass of Al / 3.
distractor_logic: Multiplying by Faraday's constant mixes charge units into a mass-based quantity, which is dimensionally wrong.
Dividing by Avogadro's number would give an absurdly tiny mass per particle, not the equivalent weight concept used here.
Multiplying (instead of dividing) by n would give an oversized, physically meaningless value.

questions.question: During the electrolysis of molten NaCl, which product forms at the cathode?
questions.explanation: In molten NaCl electrolysis, Na<sup>+</sup> ions migrate to the cathode and are reduced to Na metal (Na<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> → Na), while Cl<sup>-</sup> is oxidised to Cl<sub>2</sub> at the anode.
questions.hint: Cathode = reduction; which ion in molten NaCl is capable of being reduced?
distractor_logic: H<sub>2</sub> gas would only be a cathode product if water were present, as in aqueous electrolysis, not molten salt electrolysis.
NaOH would form in the electrolysis of an aqueous NaCl solution (via water-related reactions), not molten NaCl, where no water is present.
Cl<sub>2</sub> is the anode product, formed by oxidation of Cl<sup>-</sup>, not at the cathode.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a primary battery (non-rechargeable)?
questions.explanation: The dry cell (Leclanché cell), used in torches and remotes, is a classic primary battery: once its chemical reactants are consumed, it cannot be recharged and must be discarded.
questions.hint: Primary cells power one-time use devices like flashlights, unlike rechargeable secondary cells.
distractor_logic: Nickel-cadmium cells are rechargeable secondary batteries commonly used in power tools.
Lithium-ion batteries, used in phones and laptops, are rechargeable secondary batteries.
The lead storage battery (used in cars) is a well-known rechargeable secondary battery.

questions.question: In a lead storage battery, what is the material used for the cathode?
questions.explanation: The cathode of a lead storage battery is lead dioxide (PbO<sub>2</sub>), which gets reduced during discharge, while the anode is spongy lead (Pb), which gets oxidised.
questions.hint: Cathode material must be capable of being reduced — PbO<sub>2</sub> contains Pb in the +4 state, which can be reduced to +2.
distractor_logic: Lead sulfate is the product formed at both electrodes during discharge, not the starting cathode material.
Dilute sulfuric acid is the electrolyte, not an electrode material.
Spongy lead is the anode material, the site of oxidation, not the cathode.

questions.question: A fuel cell that combines H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> to directly generate electricity has water as its main by-product; this makes it attractive mainly because
options: It is a pollution-free energy conversion device with high efficiency
It only works at extremely low temperatures
questions.explanation: The H<sub>2</sub>-O<sub>2</sub> fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy with high efficiency, and its only by-product is water, making it an environmentally clean energy source (notably used in spacecraft).
questions.hint: Recall its famous use in providing both electricity and drinking water on space missions.
distractor_logic: A major advantage of fuel cells is that they can operate continuously as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied, unlike primary batteries.
Water is the actual by-product, which is non-toxic, not a pollutant.
Fuel cells typically operate around 70–140°C or higher depending on design, not extremely low temperatures.

questions.question: Rechargeable batteries are also called
questions.explanation: Secondary cells (like Ni-Cd and lead storage batteries) can be recharged by passing current in the reverse direction, reversing the cell reaction, unlike primary cells which are single-use.
questions.hint: The 'secondary' reaction here refers to the reverse (recharging) process being possible.
distractor_logic: Primary cells are the single-use, non-rechargeable type — the opposite of what's being described.
Concentration cells generate EMF from a concentration difference, an unrelated classification.
Reference cells (like SHE) are used to measure potentials, unrelated to rechargeability.

questions.question: Corrosion of iron (commonly called rusting) is fundamentally an example of a/an
options: Simple dissolution process with no redox involved
Purely physical process with no chemical change
Electrochemical process involving oxidation and reduction
questions.explanation: Rusting is an electrochemical process in which iron is oxidised at anodic spots on the metal surface, and atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> is reduced at cathodic spots, in the presence of moisture acting as the electrolyte.
questions.hint: Think of the metal surface itself as a tiny short-circuited galvanic cell.
distractor_logic: There is real oxidation of the metal and reduction of oxygen involved; it is not a simple non-redox dissolution.
It is fundamentally a chemical (electrochemical) change, not purely physical.
Corrosion does not involve any nuclear transformation; it is an ordinary chemical/electrochemical process.

questions.question: In the rusting of iron, which substance is reduced at the cathodic regions of the metal surface?
questions.explanation: At cathodic regions, dissolved atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> is reduced (in the presence of H<sup>+</sup>) to form water: O<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 4e<sup>-</sup> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O, consuming the electrons released by iron oxidation elsewhere.
questions.hint: The overall process needs an oxidising agent to accept the electrons that iron loses — what's abundant in air?
distractor_logic: Fe<sup>3+</sup> formation is a later step in rust formation (Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>·xH<sub>2</sub>O), not the primary cathodic reduction reaction.
Under normal rusting conditions, oxygen reduction is favoured over the evolution of H<sub>2</sub> gas from water.
Iron itself is oxidised (loses electrons) at anodic spots, not reduced at cathodic ones.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'galvanisation' as an anti-corrosion technique?
options: Painting iron with a decorative, non-metallic coating only
Coating iron with a layer of a more easily oxidised metal like zinc
Heating iron to extremely high temperatures to harden it
Mixing iron with carbon to make it non-reactive
questions.explanation: Galvanisation coats iron with zinc, a more reactive (more easily oxidised) metal; zinc preferentially corrodes and also provides a physical barrier, protecting the underlying iron even if the coating is scratched (sacrificial protection).
questions.hint: Zinc is more reactive than iron and gets oxidised preferentially, protecting the iron underneath.
distractor_logic: Ordinary decorative paint provides only a physical barrier without the sacrificial electrochemical protection that zinc coating provides.
Heat treatment (hardening) is a metallurgical process unrelated to corrosion prevention by coating.
Mixing with carbon produces steel, which actually can still corrode; this is not the mechanism of galvanisation.

questions.topic: Gibbs Energy, EMF and Equilibrium Constant
questions.question: For a spontaneous redox reaction at equilibrium, which of these is true?
questions.explanation: At equilibrium, the net driving force vanishes, so the actual cell potential E<sub>cell</sub> = 0 and correspondingly ΔG = 0 (using ΔG = −nFE<sub>cell</sub>), even though E°<sub>cell</sub> and ΔG° remain fixed, non-zero reference quantities.
questions.hint: Distinguish carefully between the 'standard' quantities (E°, ΔG°) and the 'actual, instantaneous' quantities (E, ΔG) at equilibrium.
distractor_logic: ΔG° is a fixed thermodynamic quantity related to ln K, and is generally non-zero unless K = 1.
E°<sub>cell</sub> is a fixed reference value tied to K, not necessarily zero, even though the instantaneous E<sub>cell</sub> is zero at equilibrium.

questions.question: The resistance of a 0.01 M weak monobasic acid solution is 250 Ω in a cell with cell constant 0.80 cm<sup>-1</sup>. If Λ<sub>m</sub>° for the acid is 380 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>, calculate the degree of dissociation (α).
questions.explanation: G = 1/250 = 0.004 S; κ = G × cell constant = 0.004 × 0.80 = 0.0032 S cm<sup>-1</sup>; Λ<sub>m</sub> = 1000κ/C = 1000(0.0032)/0.01 = 320 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>; α = Λ<sub>m</sub>/Λ<sub>m</sub>° = 320/380 ≈ 0.842.
questions.hint: Chain the calculation step by step: resistance → conductance → specific conductivity → molar conductivity → degree of dissociation.
distractor_logic: This is roughly half the correct value, consistent with a missed factor of 2 somewhere in the conductance or cell-constant step.
This is off by a factor of 10, consistent with a decimal-point slip converting κ to Λ<sub>m</sub>.
This exceeds 1, which is physically impossible for a degree of dissociation, indicating an inverted ratio (Λ<sub>m</sub>°/Λ<sub>m</sub> instead of Λ<sub>m</sub>/Λ<sub>m</sub>°) or arithmetic slip.

questions.question: A 0.02 M solution of a weak acid has Λ<sub>m</sub> = 9.83 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and Λ<sub>m</sub>° = 390.5 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate K<sub>a</sub> using K<sub>a</sub> = Cα<sup>2</sup>/(1−α).
questions.hint: Calculate α first (as a ratio, not a percentage), then substitute carefully into the Ostwald dilution law expression, keeping the (1−α) denominator.
distractor_logic: This drastically overestimates α itself (treating it more like 0.25 instead of 0.025), producing a K<sub>a</sub> two orders of magnitude too large.
This is the numerator Cα<sup>2</sup> alone, without dividing by the (1−α) denominator, though a decimal-scale mismatch also creeps in.
This is close to the correct value but omits the (1−α) correction in the denominator (using 1 in its place), giving a slightly smaller result.

questions.question: A conductivity cell shows resistance 220 Ω when filled with 0.01 M KCl (specific conductance = 0.00141 S cm<sup>-1</sup>). The same cell shows resistance 55 Ω for 0.01 M of an unknown salt solution. Calculate the molar conductivity of the unknown salt.
questions.explanation: Cell constant = κ(KCl) × R(KCl) = 0.00141 × 220 = 0.3102 cm<sup>-1</sup>. For the unknown: G = 1/55 = 0.01818 S; κ = 0.01818 × 0.3102 ≈ 0.005640 S cm<sup>-1</sup>; Λ<sub>m</sub> = 1000 × 0.005640/0.01 = 564.0 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
questions.hint: This is a two-stage problem: first find the cell constant from the known KCl data, then apply that same cell constant to the unknown solution's resistance.
distractor_logic: This overshoots by exactly double, consistent with a doubling error somewhere in the resistance-to-conductance conversion.
This is roughly a factor of 20 too small, consistent with skipping the unit conversion (×1000) in the final molar conductivity step.
This treats the KCl specific conductance itself as if it directly applied to the unknown, skipping the cell-constant determination step entirely.

questions.question: Λ<sub>m</sub>° values: HCl = 426.2, CH<sub>3</sub>COONa = 91.0, NaCl = 126.5 (all S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>). A 0.001 M acetic acid solution has Λ<sub>m</sub> = 48.15 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate the degree of dissociation of acetic acid at this concentration.
questions.explanation: Λ<sub>m</sub>°(CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) = Λ<sub>m</sub>°(HCl) + Λ<sub>m</sub>°(CH<sub>3</sub>COONa) − Λ<sub>m</sub>°(NaCl) = 426.2 + 91.0 − 126.5 = 390.7 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. α = Λ<sub>m</sub>/Λ<sub>m</sub>° = 48.15/390.7 ≈ 0.123.
questions.hint: First use Kohlrausch's law to reconstruct Λ<sub>m</sub>° for acetic acid from the three strong-electrolyte values, then take the ratio to the given Λ<sub>m</sub>.
distractor_logic: This mistakes α for (1 − the correct value), a common inversion error when reading dissociation vs association fractions.
This roughly doubles the correct α, consistent with an error in computing Λ<sub>m</sub>° (perhaps forgetting to subtract the NaCl term, giving too small a Λ<sub>m</sub>° and hence too large an α).
This is roughly a quarter of the correct value, consistent with using an incorrect (too large) Λ<sub>m</sub>° from mishandling the Kohlrausch combination.

questions.question: For a weak monobasic acid, Λ<sub>m</sub> at C = 0.001 M is 200 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>, and Λ<sub>m</sub>° = 400 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. Using Ostwald's dilution law (K<sub>a</sub> = Cα<sup>2</sup>/(1−α)), calculate K<sub>a</sub>.
questions.explanation: α = Λ<sub>m</sub>/Λ<sub>m</sub>° = 200/400 = 0.5. K<sub>a</sub> = 0.001 × (0.5)<sup>2</sup>/(1−0.5) = 0.001 × 0.25/0.5 = 0.00025/0.5 = 5.0 × 10<sup>-4</sup>.
questions.hint: With α = 0.5 exactly, the (1−α) term is also exactly 0.5 — a clean simplification worth spotting before grinding through the arithmetic.
distractor_logic: This is double the correct value, perhaps from mistakenly halving the denominator's effect instead of applying it.
This uses an incorrect α value (0.2 or similar) rather than the correctly computed 0.5.
This omits the (1−α) denominator, using Cα<sup>2</sup> alone (0.001 × 0.25 = 2.5 × 10<sup>-4</sup>), which is only valid as an approximation when α is very small, not at α = 0.5.

questions.question: Given λ°(H<sup>+</sup>) = 349.6 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and λ°(CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>) = 40.9 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>, and a measured Λ<sub>m</sub> of 16.18 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> for 0.01 M acetic acid, calculate the percentage dissociation.
questions.explanation: Λ<sub>m</sub>°(CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. α = 16.18/390.5 ≈ 0.0414, i.e., 4.14% dissociation.
questions.hint: First add the two limiting ionic conductivities to get Λ<sub>m</sub>°, then express the ratio Λ<sub>m</sub>/Λ<sub>m</sub>° as a percentage.
distractor_logic: This is exactly double the correct percentage, consistent with a factor-of-2 slip somewhere in the ratio calculation.
This is exactly ten times too large, consistent with a decimal-point misplacement when converting the ratio to a percentage.
This is exactly half the correct percentage — the mirror image of the doubling error that produces 8.28% instead.

questions.question: Three electrolytic cells containing AgNO<sub>3</sub>, CuSO<sub>4</sub>, and AlCl<sub>3</sub> solutions are connected in series. If 1.08 g of Ag is deposited (Ag = 108 g/mol, n = 1), calculate the mass of Al deposited in the same time. (Al = 27 g/mol, n = 3)
questions.explanation: Moles of Ag = 1.08/108 = 0.01 mol = moles of electrons passed (since n = 1 for Ag). For Al (n = 3), moles of Al = 0.01/3 ≈ 0.00333 mol; mass = 0.00333 × 27 = 0.09 g.
questions.hint: In cells connected in series, the same number of moles of electrons passes through each; only the valence factor n differs between the metals.
distractor_logic: This treats moles of Al as equal to moles of Ag directly (ignoring the different n values), overstating the mass threefold.
This uses n = 1 for Al instead of the correct n = 3, again overstating the mass.
This underestimates further, consistent with an additional factor-of-3 error compounding the n mismatch.

questions.question: A current of 2 A is passed for 2 hours through molten Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> to produce aluminium, but the process operates at only 80% current efficiency. Calculate the actual mass of Al deposited. (Al = 27 g/mol, n = 3, F = 96500 C/mol)
questions.explanation: Total charge Q = It = 2 × 2 × 3600 = 14400 C. Effective (useful) charge = 0.80 × 14400 = 11520 C. Moles of electrons = 11520/96500 = 0.1194 mol; moles of Al = 0.1194/3 = 0.0398 mol; mass = 0.0398 × 27 ≈ 1.074 g.
questions.hint: Apply the current efficiency as a scaling factor on the total charge before converting to moles of metal, not after.
distractor_logic: This forgets the 80% efficiency correction entirely, computing as if all the charge were used productively.
This applies the efficiency factor in the wrong direction (dividing by 0.80 instead of multiplying), overstating the mass.
This applies an incorrect (too low) efficiency value in the calculation, understating the mass.

questions.question: Equal charge is passed through two cells in series: one containing CuSO<sub>4</sub> (Cu = 63.5 g/mol, n = 2) and the other AgNO<sub>3</sub> (Ag = 108 g/mol, n = 1). If 3.175 g of Cu is deposited, find the mass of Ag deposited in the other cell.
questions.explanation: Moles of Cu = 3.175/63.5 = 0.05 mol; moles of electrons = 0.05 × 2 = 0.1 mol (same charge passes through both cells in series). Moles of Ag = 0.1/1 = 0.1 mol; mass of Ag = 0.1 × 108 = 10.8 g.
questions.hint: Equal charge means equal moles of electrons in both cells; convert via each metal's own valence factor separately.
distractor_logic: This wrongly assumes equal moles of metal are deposited (ignoring the different n values), rather than equal moles of electrons.
This doubles the correct answer, perhaps from doubling the already-correct electron count once more by mistake.
This is exactly half the correct value, consistent with forgetting to double the moles of electrons via Cu's n = 2 factor.

questions.question: A metal M forms M<sup>3+</sup> ions in solution. When a current of 3 A is passed for 1930 seconds through a solution of its salt, 1.8 g of the metal is deposited. Calculate the atomic mass of M. (F = 96500 C/mol)
questions.explanation: Q = It = 3 × 1930 = 5790 C; moles of electrons = 5790/96500 = 0.06 mol; moles of M = 0.06/3 = 0.02 mol (since n = 3); atomic mass = mass/moles = 1.8/0.02 = 90 g/mol.
questions.hint: Work backward from charge to moles of electrons, then to moles of metal (using n = 3), and finally divide the given mass by moles to get atomic mass.
distractor_logic: This results from forgetting to divide moles of electrons by n = 3 (treating moles of M as equal to moles of electrons), understating the atomic mass threefold.
This is exactly two-thirds of the correct value, consistent with a partial (but incomplete) application of the n = 3 correction.
This overstates atomic mass threefold, perhaps from an inverted use of the valence factor.

questions.question: In the lead storage battery discharge reaction Pb(s) + PbO<sub>2</sub>(s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq) → 2PbSO<sub>4</sub>(s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O(l), if 0.5 mol of Pb reacts at the anode, how many moles of electrons flow through the external circuit?
questions.explanation: At the anode, Pb → Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup>, so each mole of Pb releases 2 moles of electrons. For 0.5 mol Pb, electrons released = 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 mol, which flow through the external circuit to reduce PbO<sub>2</sub> at the cathode.
questions.hint: Identify the anode half-reaction first and note the electron count per mole of Pb oxidised (n = 2).
distractor_logic: This doubles the correct value, perhaps from double-counting electrons at both electrodes rather than just the anode's release.
This quarters the correct value, consistent with a compounded halving-type error.
This assumes a 1:1 mole-to-electron ratio, missing that each Pb atom releases 2 electrons (n = 2), not 1.

questions.question: In a H<sub>2</sub>-O<sub>2</sub> fuel cell, calculate the total charge (in coulombs) produced when exactly 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub> gas is completely consumed at the anode. (F = 96500 C/mol)
questions.explanation: The anode reaction is H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>-</sup> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>-</sup> (or equivalently H<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup>), releasing 2 moles of electrons per mole of H<sub>2</sub>. Charge = 2 × 96500 = 193000 C.
questions.hint: Each H<sub>2</sub> molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms, each losing one electron, so n = 2 per mole of H<sub>2</sub>, not 1.
distractor_logic: This uses n = 1 instead of the correct n = 2 for H<sub>2</sub> oxidation, understating the charge by half.
This overstates the charge by using n = 4 instead of n = 2, doubling the correct value.
This is exactly a quarter of the correct value, likely from using n = 0.5 or a similarly mis-set electron count.

questions.question: A device requires approximately 6.0 V to operate. Comparing lead storage cells (≈2.0 V each) against Ni-Cd cells (≈1.2 V each) connected in series, how many of each are needed, and which uses fewer cells?
options: 3 lead storage cells vs 5 Ni-Cd cells; lead storage uses fewer
3 lead storage cells vs 6 Ni-Cd cells; Ni-Cd uses fewer
2 lead storage cells vs 4 Ni-Cd cells; lead storage uses fewer
5 lead storage cells vs 3 Ni-Cd cells; Ni-Cd uses fewer
questions.explanation: Number of cells = required voltage ÷ per-cell voltage. Lead storage: 6.0/2.0 = 3 cells; Ni-Cd: 6.0/1.2 = 5 cells. Since 3 < 5, the lead storage arrangement uses fewer cells for the same total voltage.
questions.hint: Divide the target voltage by each battery type's typical single-cell voltage separately, then compare the two cell counts.
distractor_logic: This correctly finds 3 lead cells but miscalculates the Ni-Cd count as 6 (implying exactly 1.0 V per cell) rather than the correct ~5 (at 1.2 V per cell), and wrongly concludes Ni-Cd is more efficient.
This uses an incorrect number of lead cells (2 instead of 3, i.e., assuming 3 V per cell rather than the actual ~2.0 V).
This swaps the two totals and reverses the conclusion about which type needs fewer cells.

questions.question: A steel structure experiences an estimated corrosion current of 2 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A spread over its surface. Estimate the mass of iron lost per year due to this corrosion current, treating it as a Faraday's-law process. (Fe = 56 g/mol, n = 2, F = 96500 C/mol; 1 year ≈ 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s)
questions.explanation: Q = It = 2 × 10<sup>-3</sup> × 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> = 63000 C; moles of electrons = 63000/96500 ≈ 0.6528 mol; moles of Fe = 0.6528/2 ≈ 0.3264 mol (n = 2 for Fe<sup>2+</sup>); mass = 0.3264 × 56 ≈ 18.28 g.
questions.hint: Treat the corrosion current exactly like an electrolysis current in Faraday's law, using n = 2 for Fe → Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup>.
distractor_logic: This doubles the correct value, perhaps from using n = 1 instead of n = 2.
This is a tenth of the correct value, consistent with a decimal-point slip in converting seconds per year.
This is exactly half the correct value, consistent with using n = 4 instead of the correct n = 2 for iron.

questions.question: Metals P (E° = −2.71 V), Q (E° = −0.76 V), and R (E° = +0.34 V) are being considered as protective coatings for an iron structure (E°(Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe) = −0.44 V). Which metal(s) would provide sacrificial (cathodic) protection to the iron?
questions.explanation: For sacrificial protection, the coating metal must be more easily oxidised than iron, i.e., have a more negative E° than −0.44 V. Both P (−2.71 V) and Q (−0.76 V) satisfy this, so they would corrode preferentially and protect the iron; R (+0.34 V), being more noble than iron, would not.
questions.hint: Compare each candidate metal's E° against iron's −0.44 V; only more negative values qualify for sacrificial protection.
distractor_logic: This incorrectly includes R, which does not meet the sacrificial-protection criterion of being more reactive than iron.

R's potential (+0.34 V) is more positive than iron's, meaning R is less reactive than iron and would not sacrificially protect it (it would instead accelerate iron's corrosion if in electrical contact, similar to tin-plating).
Both P and Q clearly satisfy the criterion (more negative E° than iron), so at least these two do protect it; this option wrongly rules out all three.

questions.question: The corrosion current density on an iron surface is 15 µA/cm<sup>2</sup>. For a total exposed area of 200 cm<sup>2</sup>, estimate the mass of Fe corroded per day. (Fe = 56 g/mol, n = 2, F = 96500 C/mol; 1 day = 86400 s)
questions.explanation: Total current = 15 × 10<sup>-6</sup> A/cm<sup>2</sup> × 200 cm<sup>2</sup> = 3 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A. Charge in a day Q = 3 × 10<sup>-3</sup> × 86400 = 259.2 C; moles of electrons = 259.2/96500 ≈ 0.002686 mol; moles of Fe = 0.001343 mol; mass = 0.001343 × 56 ≈ 0.0752 g = 75.2 mg.
questions.hint: First convert current density to total current using the given area, then proceed through the standard Faraday's-law chain (charge → moles of electrons → moles of Fe → mass).
distractor_logic: This is exactly half the correct value, consistent with using n = 4 instead of n = 2 for iron.
This is a quarter of the correct value, consistent with a compounded area or current-density conversion error.
This doubles the correct value, likely from using n = 1 instead of n = 2.

questions.question: An iron nail is partly wound with copper wire and left in a humid, salty environment, compared to an identical plain iron nail kept in dry air. How and why does the corrosion behaviour differ?
options: The wound nail corrodes faster, but only due to humidity; the copper wire plays no additional role
The wound nail corrodes more slowly, since copper sacrificially protects the iron
There is no difference, since copper has no electrochemical effect on iron
The wound nail corrodes markedly faster, since the galvanic couple with the more noble copper and the conductive salt-moisture film both accelerate electrochemical corrosion of the iron
questions.explanation: Copper is more noble (higher E°) than iron, so contact between them sets up a galvanic couple in which iron becomes the anode and corrodes faster than it would alone; the humid, salty environment additionally provides a highly conductive electrolyte film, further accelerating the electrochemical process. Both effects compound to markedly increase corrosion versus a plain nail in dry air.
questions.hint: Consider both factors together: the metal-pairing effect (galvanic coupling) and the environmental effect (electrolyte conductivity) act simultaneously, not separately.
distractor_logic: This underestimates the situation by ignoring the additional galvanic-coupling effect from the copper wire, attributing the entire change to humidity alone.
This has the direction backwards; only a less noble metal than iron (like zinc) offers sacrificial protection — copper, being more noble, accelerates iron's corrosion instead.
This ignores the well-established electrochemical effect of dissimilar-metal contact on corrosion rates.

questions.question: For the Daniell cell (E°<sub>cell</sub> = 1.10 V, n = 2), if [Zn<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.001 M and [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.1 M at 298 K, calculate ΔG for the cell under these non-standard conditions. (F = 96500 C/mol)
questions.explanation: Q = [Zn<sup>2+</sup>]/[Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.001/0.1 = 0.01. E<sub>cell</sub> = 1.10 − (0.0591/2) log(0.01) = 1.10 − (0.02955)(−2) = 1.10 + 0.0591 = 1.1591 V. ΔG = −nFE<sub>cell</sub> = −2 × 96500 × 1.1591 ≈ −223,700 J/mol = −223.7 kJ/mol.
questions.hint: First use the Nernst equation to find the actual (non-standard) E<sub>cell</sub>, then apply ΔG = −nFE<sub>cell</sub> using this corrected value, not E°<sub>cell</sub>.
distractor_logic: This under-corrects, as if only a partial Nernst adjustment were applied.
This uses the standard ΔG° (from E°<sub>cell</sub> alone), skipping the Nernst correction for the given non-standard concentrations entirely.
This has the right general magnitude but the wrong sign, inconsistent with a clearly spontaneous, very negative E°<sub>cell</sub>-based reaction becoming even more favourable at these concentrations.

questions.question: A Daniell cell (E°<sub>cell</sub> = 1.10 V) is compared to a hypothetical galvanic corrosion couple formed between zinc and copper rivets in a humid environment. Why does the zinc corrode rapidly in the second scenario even without an external circuit or salt bridge?
options: No reaction occurs without a salt bridge, so neither metal would corrode
Corrosion is a completely different, non-electrochemical process unrelated to the Daniell cell reaction
Copper corrodes instead of zinc in this scenario, reversing the Daniell cell's direction
Direct metal-to-metal contact plus a surface moisture film acts as a short-circuited galvanic cell, letting the same spontaneous Zn/Cu reaction proceed as an uncontrolled corrosion process
questions.explanation: The thermodynamic driving force (E°<sub>cell</sub> = +1.10 V, so ΔG° is very negative) is identical to the Daniell cell; in the corrosion scenario, the moisture film substitutes for the electrolyte/salt bridge, and direct contact between the metals substitutes for the external wire, so the same spontaneous Zn-oxidation, Cu-protection reaction proceeds, just less controlled and often much faster since it isn't limited by external resistance.
questions.hint: The salt bridge and external wire in a lab cell are really just providing a completable circuit — anything else that completes that circuit (like a moisture film and direct contact) can drive the same reaction.
distractor_logic: A salt bridge is a lab convenience for separating half-cells; when metals are in direct contact with a shared electrolyte film (as in corrosion), no separate salt bridge is needed for the reaction to proceed.
Corrosion is fundamentally the same type of electrochemical (redox) process as a galvanic cell reaction, just occurring in an uncontrolled, localised way on the metal surface.
Zinc remains the more reactive (more negative E°) metal in both scenarios and is oxidised in both; copper is protected/reduced, not the other way around.

questions.question: The overall reaction in a Daniell cell, Zn(s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cu(s), and the overall discharge reaction of a lead storage battery both release electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction. What is the key structural difference that makes the lead storage battery rechargeable while a simple Daniell cell is not typically used that way?
options: The lead storage battery does not involve any redox chemistry, unlike the Daniell cell

In the lead storage battery, both the oxidised and reduced products (PbSO<sub>4</sub> at both electrodes) remain attached to their respective electrodes and can be reconverted by reversing the current, whereas Daniell cell products (aqueous Zn<sup>2+</sup>, solid Cu) can diffuse away, making clean reversal impractical
Lead storage batteries use only one electrode material, unlike the two-electrode Daniell cell
The Daniell cell reaction is not thermodynamically reversible under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Rechargeability requires that the discharge products stay localised near their original electrode positions so that passing current in reverse can reform the original reactants efficiently; PbSO<sub>4</sub> deposits directly on both lead-based electrodes, enabling this, whereas the soluble Zn<sup>2+</sup> ions in a Daniell cell can diffuse throughout the solution, making a clean, efficient reversal impractical in the simple two-compartment design.
questions.hint: Think about where the reaction products physically end up in each cell, not just whether the reaction itself could in principle run backward.
distractor_logic: Both cells are fundamentally redox (electrochemical) reactions; this option misdescribes the lead storage battery's chemistry.
The lead storage battery, like the Daniell cell, has two distinct electrodes (Pb and PbO<sub>2</sub>), not just one.

In principle, any spontaneous cell reaction can be reversed by applying a sufficient external EMF (this is electrolysis); the real obstacle for the Daniell cell is practical, not fundamental impossibility.

questions.question: A student wants to build a galvanic cell using the redox couple Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>/Cr<sup>3+</sup> (E° = +1.33 V) as the cathode and Sn<sup>4+</sup>/Sn<sup>2+</sup> (E° = +0.15 V) as the anode. Using log K = nE°<sub>cell</sub>/0.0591 with the correctly balanced n = 6 for this reaction, is this reaction likely to go essentially to completion?
options: It cannot be determined without knowing the reaction rate (kinetics)
Yes, but only because n happens to be an even number
No; E°<sub>cell</sub> is negative, so the reaction barely proceeds
Yes; E°<sub>cell</sub> = 1.18 V gives an extremely large K, so the reaction proceeds essentially to completion
questions.explanation: E°<sub>cell</sub> = 1.33 − 0.15 = 1.18 V, clearly positive. With n = 6, log K = (6 × 1.18)/0.0591 ≈ 119.8, an astronomically large K, meaning the equilibrium lies overwhelmingly toward products — the reaction proceeds essentially to completion under standard conditions.
questions.hint: A large positive E°<sub>cell</sub>, combined with a sizeable n, produces an enormous K via the exponential relationship between log K and E°<sub>cell</sub>.
distractor_logic: Thermodynamics (via K) tells us the reaction is strongly favoured at equilibrium; while kinetics governs how fast it gets there, the extent (completeness) at equilibrium is a thermodynamic question this data can answer.
The evenness of n is not what determines completeness; it is the magnitude and sign of E°<sub>cell</sub> (and hence log K) that matters.
E°<sub>cell</sub> here is clearly positive (1.18 V), not negative; this option misreads the sign.

questions.question: In a fuel cell (H<sub>2</sub>/O<sub>2</sub>) generating electricity from a spontaneous redox reaction, and in the electrolysis of water (using electricity to split water into H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>), the chemical species involved are essentially the reverse of each other. What does this reveal about the sign of ΔG for each process?
options: ΔG is negative for both processes, since both involve water and hydrogen/oxygen
ΔG is zero for both, since they are exact reverses of one another
ΔG is positive for the fuel cell and negative for electrolysis
ΔG is negative for the spontaneous fuel-cell reaction and positive for the non-spontaneous electrolysis reaction, which is exactly its reverse
questions.explanation: Since electrolysis of water is the reverse reaction of the fuel cell's spontaneous combination of H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>, and ΔG reverses sign for the reverse reaction, the fuel cell (spontaneous, generates electricity) has ΔG < 0, while electrolysis (needs external electricity, non-spontaneous) has ΔG > 0.
questions.hint: A reaction and its exact reverse always have ΔG values equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.
distractor_logic: This claims both are negative, which would mean both directions of the very same equilibrium are spontaneous simultaneously — thermodynamically impossible.
ΔG being exactly zero for both would mean neither process actually requires or releases net energy, contradicting the fact that electrolysis clearly requires external electrical input.
This reverses the correct assignment: the fuel cell (spontaneous) must have negative ΔG, and electrolysis (requiring external energy input) must have positive ΔG, not the other way around.

questions.question: Using E°(Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>) = +0.77 V and E°(I<sub>2</sub>/I<sup>-</sup>) = +0.54 V, calculate the equilibrium constant K (at 298 K) for the reaction 2Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + 2I<sup>-</sup>(aq) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + I<sub>2</sub>(s). (n = 2)
questions.explanation: E°<sub>cell</sub> = E°(Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>) − E°(I<sub>2</sub>/I<sup>-</sup>) = 0.77 − 0.54 = 0.23 V. log K = nE°<sub>cell</sub>/0.0591 = (2 × 0.23)/0.0591 ≈ 7.78, so K ≈ 10<sup>7.78</sup> ≈ 6.07 × 10<sup>7</sup>, favouring the forward reaction strongly.
questions.hint: First identify which couple acts as cathode (the one with the higher E°) to find E°<sub>cell</sub> correctly, then apply the log K relation with n = 2.
distractor_logic: This underestimates log K, consistent with an arithmetic slip giving log K ≈ 4.1 instead of 7.78.
This is far too small, consistent with mistakenly using n = 1 and a smaller E°<sub>cell</sub> in the log K formula.
This severely underestimates the exponential relationship, treating log K as roughly 1.4 rather than 7.78.

questions.question: In a fuel cell, the cathode reaction O<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 4e<sup>-</sup> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (E° = +1.23 V) also describes the cathodic half-reaction responsible for the corrosion (rusting) of iron in neutral, aerated water. What connects these two seemingly different processes?
options: The two reactions are exact reverses of each other
Corrosion never involves oxygen reduction; only the fuel cell reaction does
They are unrelated; the fuel cell reaction cannot occur during rusting since no external circuit is present

Both use atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> reduction as the electron-accepting (cathodic) half-reaction, driven by the same thermodynamically favourable couple, whether the electrons come from H<sub>2</sub> gas (fuel cell) or from iron being oxidised (corrosion)
questions.explanation: The O<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O couple's high standard reduction potential (+1.23 V) makes it a strong, universally available oxidising half-reaction; in a fuel cell it consumes electrons released by H<sub>2</sub> oxidation, while during rusting it consumes electrons released by iron oxidation at nearby anodic sites — in both cases, the same cathodic chemistry (O<sub>2</sub> reduction) is what drives the overall spontaneous process forward.
questions.hint: Focus on what the O<sub>2</sub> reduction half-reaction is actually doing in each case: accepting electrons from a different oxidation half-reaction each time.
distractor_logic: Both reactions consume O<sub>2</sub> as the oxidising agent (the same direction, reduction), so they are not reverses of one another.
Oxygen reduction at cathodic regions is, in fact, the standard mechanism proposed for atmospheric rusting of iron, not something excluded from it.
An external circuit is not strictly required; corrosion works as a 'short-circuited' galvanic process on the metal surface itself, still using the same O<sub>2</sub> reduction cathodic half-reaction.

questions.question: The electrochemical series places Li (E° = −3.05 V) near the top (most negative) and F<sub>2</sub> (E° = +2.87 V) near the bottom (most positive). If lithium metal were used as a sacrificial anode to protect a steel pipeline (E°(Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe) = −0.44 V), would this be a technically sound (though likely impractical) choice compared to magnesium (E° = −2.36 V)?
options: No, because Li has a positive reduction potential, making it a poor reducing agent
Yes, but only because Li and Fe have identical reduction potentials
No, because Li is less reactive than Fe and cannot act as a sacrificial anode at all

Technically yes, since Li is even more reactive (more negative E°) than Mg and would corrode preferentially even faster, though its high reactivity with water/air makes it impractical and hazardous in practice
questions.explanation: Since E°(Li<sup>+</sup>/Li) is more negative than both E°(Mg<sup>2+</sup>/Mg) and E°(Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe), lithium would indeed be oxidised even more readily than magnesium, technically satisfying the sacrificial-anode requirement; however, lithium's extreme reactivity with moisture and air (and its cost) makes it a poor practical engineering choice compared to magnesium or zinc.
questions.hint: Separate the thermodynamic question (would it work, based on E°?) from the practical engineering question (should it be used?).
distractor_logic: Lithium's reduction potential is strongly negative (−3.05 V), not positive; this option misstates the sign entirely.
Li (−3.05 V) and Fe (−0.44 V) have clearly different potentials, not identical ones.
Li's reduction potential (−3.05 V) is far more negative than Fe's (−0.44 V), meaning Li is dramatically more reactive than iron, the opposite of this claim.

questions.question: Given E°(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu) = +0.34 V and using the Nernst equation, at what [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] would the electrode potential become exactly equal to that of the SHE (0.00 V) at 298 K? (n = 2)
questions.explanation: Setting E = 0: 0 = 0.34 − (0.0591/2) log(1/[Cu<sup>2+</sup>]); rearranging, log(1/[Cu<sup>2+</sup>]) = 0.34/(0.02955) ≈ 11.506, so [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 10<sup>-11.506</sup> ≈ 3.1 × 10<sup>-12</sup> M — an extremely dilute concentration, illustrating just how strongly concentration must drop to offset a fairly large standard potential.
questions.hint: Set E = 0 in the Nernst equation and solve algebraically for log[Cu<sup>2+</sup>], then convert back from the logarithm.
distractor_logic: This is not derived from solving the equation at all; it simply restates the numeric value of E° itself, mistaken for a concentration.
At [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 1 M, the potential simply equals E° = 0.34 V, not 0 V; this is the standard-state value, not the answer to this question.
This underestimates how dilute the solution must be by many orders of magnitude, consistent with mis-scaling the exponent in the final step.

questions.question: The MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> titration reaction (E°<sub>cell</sub> = 0.74 V, n = 5) is run with [MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>] = 1 M, [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 1 M, [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1 M, but with [Mn<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.01 M and [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.1 M (reaction partially proceeded). Calculate E<sub>cell</sub> under these conditions at 298 K.
questions.explanation: Q = ([Mn<sup>2+</sup>][Fe<sup>3+</sup>]<sup>5</sup>)/([MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>][Fe<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>5</sup>[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>8</sup>) = (0.01 × 0.1<sup>5</sup>)/(1 × 1<sup>5</sup> × 1<sup>8</sup>) = 1 × 10<sup>-7</sup>. E<sub>cell</sub> = 0.74 − (0.0591/5) log(10<sup>-7</sup>) = 0.74 − (0.01182)(−7) = 0.74 + 0.0827 ≈ 0.823 V.
questions.hint: Build Q very carefully using the full balanced equation's stoichiometric powers for every species, including [H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>8</sup>, even though [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1 M here simplifies that particular term to 1.
distractor_logic: This overcorrects, consistent with using an incorrect (too large) magnitude for the log Q term.
This is simply the unadjusted standard value, ignoring the Nernst correction from the partially reacted concentrations.
This applies the correction with the wrong sign, as though Q were greater than 1 rather than much less than 1.

questions.question: A weak monoprotic acid HA has α = 0.042 at C = 0.1 M (from conductivity measurements). If a hydrogen electrode were placed in this solution at 298 K and 1 bar H<sub>2</sub>, what would its potential be, given [H<sup>+</sup>] = Cα?
questions.explanation: [H<sup>+</sup>] = Cα = 0.1 × 0.042 = 0.0042 M, so pH = −log(0.0042) ≈ 2.377. Using the hydrogen-electrode shortcut E = −0.0591 × pH = −0.0591 × 2.377 ≈ −0.1405 V.
questions.hint: First use the given degree of dissociation to find [H<sup>+</sup>] = Cα, then apply E = −0.0591 × pH for the hydrogen electrode.
distractor_logic: This corresponds to pH = 1 rather than the correct ≈2.38, an underuse of the actual [H<sup>+</sup>] value.
This would only be correct for a strong acid at [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1 M (pH = 0), ignoring both the weak-acid dissociation and the resulting non-zero potential.
This significantly overstates the acidity implied by α = 0.042 at C = 0.1 M, corresponding to a much lower (more acidic) pH than is actually the case.

questions.question: A lead storage battery cell (nominal E°<sub>cell</sub> ≈ 2.0 V) becomes significantly discharged, with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> concentration dropping well below its initial value. Based on the Nernst equation applied to the overall discharge reaction (which consumes H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> as a reactant), how does the actual (measured) cell voltage change as discharge proceeds?
options: It increases above 2.0 V as discharge proceeds
It gradually decreases below the nominal value, since decreasing reactant (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) concentration increases Q, lowering E<sub>cell</sub> via the Nernst equation
It immediately drops to 0 V the moment discharge begins
It remains exactly constant at 2.0 V throughout discharge, regardless of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> concentration
questions.explanation: Since H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a reactant that gets consumed during discharge (forming PbSO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O), its concentration falls, increasing the reaction quotient Q; by the Nernst equation, E<sub>cell</sub> = E°<sub>cell</sub> − (0.0591/n) log Q, a larger Q makes E<sub>cell</sub> progressively smaller — this is exactly why measuring electrolyte density (and hence voltage) is a practical way to gauge a lead-acid battery's charge state.
questions.hint: Identify H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>'s role as a reactant in the discharge reaction, then apply the same Nernst logic used for any other galvanic cell as concentrations shift.
distractor_logic: This contradicts the Nernst equation's clear prediction that increasing Q (from falling reactant concentration) should decrease, not increase, the cell voltage.
The voltage decreases gradually as discharge proceeds, not instantaneously to zero at the very start; a battery still delivers useful voltage through most of its discharge cycle.
Real cells are not ideal — the Nernst equation predicts a real, measurable voltage drop as reactant concentrations change during use, which is precisely why battery voltage sags as it discharges.

questions.question: A conductivity experiment shows a certain weak acid is 4.14% dissociated at 0.01 M (using Λ<sub>m</sub>° = 390.5 S cm<sup>2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>). Separately, a hydrogen electrode dipped in this same solution shows a potential of −0.083 V at 298 K and 1 bar H<sub>2</sub>. Are these two independent measurements consistent with each other?
options: No comparison is possible since conductivity and electrode potential measure unrelated properties
They are consistent only if the acid is assumed to be a strong acid instead

Yes; [H<sup>+</sup>] from α is 0.01 × 0.0414 = 4.14 × 10<sup>-4</sup> M, giving pH ≈ 3.38, and E = −0.0591 × 3.38 ≈ −0.200 V, which is notably different from −0.083 V, so the two measurements are actually NOT consistent, suggesting an error in one of them
Yes, they match exactly, confirming both measurements are correct
questions.explanation: Checking the numbers: [H<sup>+</sup>] = Cα = 0.01 × 0.0414 = 4.14 × 10<sup>-4</sup> M, so pH = −log(4.14 × 10<sup>-4</sup>) ≈ 3.38, giving a predicted hydrogen-electrode potential of about −0.0591 × 3.38 ≈ −0.200 V — this does not match the stated measured value of −0.083 V, so the two given data points are inconsistent with each other (this discrepancy itself is the answer the question is testing: spotting the mismatch through calculation, not assuming agreement).
questions.hint: Don't just assume the two experimental techniques must agree — actually calculate the predicted potential from the conductivity-derived pH and compare it numerically to the stated electrode reading.
distractor_logic: Both conductivity and electrode potential ultimately depend on the same underlying [H<sup>+</sup>], so they are directly comparable and can be cross-checked against each other, as this problem demonstrates.
Assuming the acid is strong would predict [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.01 M (pH = 2), giving yet another different (and still inconsistent) potential value, so this doesn't resolve the mismatch either.
Two measurements agreeing 'exactly' would require the actual calculation to confirm it; performing that calculation here reveals a clear mismatch instead, not agreement.

questions.question: For the disproportionation-driven corrosion protection scheme, if a galvanic cell built from Mg (E° = −2.36 V) and Fe (E° = −0.44 V) has n = 2, calculate ΔG° (in kJ/mol) for the reaction Mg(s) + Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) → Mg<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Fe(s), and state whether this supports Mg's use as a sacrificial anode.
options: ΔG° ≈ +370.6 kJ/mol; positive, meaning Mg cannot protect Fe
ΔG° ≈ −370.6 kJ/mol; strongly negative, confirming Mg is thermodynamically favoured to be oxidised in preference to Fe
questions.explanation: E°<sub>cell</sub> = E°(Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe) − E°(Mg<sup>2+</sup>/Mg) = −0.44 − (−2.36) = +1.92 V (Fe<sup>2+</sup> is reduced, Mg is oxidised). ΔG° = −nFE°<sub>cell</sub> = −2 × 96500 × 1.92 ≈ −370,600 J/mol = −370.6 kJ/mol, a strongly negative value confirming the reaction (and hence Mg's sacrificial role) is thermodynamically very favourable.
questions.hint: Correctly identify which couple is reduced (cathode) and which is oxidised (anode) from the reaction as written, then apply E°<sub>cell</sub> = E°<sub>cathode</sub> − E°<sub>anode</sub>.
distractor_logic: ΔG° = 0 would mean the reaction is exactly balanced at equilibrium under standard conditions, which is inconsistent with the large potential difference between Mg and Fe couples.
This is exactly half the correct magnitude, consistent with using n = 1 instead of n = 2.
This has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign, which would incorrectly suggest Mg cannot protect Fe, contradicting well-established cathodic protection practice.

questions.question: A fuel cell reaction (2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O, E°<sub>cell</sub> = 1.23 V, n = 4) is compared with the electrolysis of water needed to reverse it. If a fuel cell delivering this reaction produces 4 mol of electrons of charge, how much electrical energy (in kJ) is theoretically released, and how does this relate to the minimum energy electrolysis would require to split the corresponding amount of water?
options: ≈ 474.8 kJ released by the fuel cell; electrolysis would require only half this energy, since it is a different process
≈ 474.8 kJ released by the fuel cell; electrolysis of the same amount of water would require at least this same amount of energy input (the exact reverse)
≈ 237.4 kJ released; electrolysis would require the same 237.4 kJ
No meaningful relationship exists between the two energies
questions.explanation: Energy released = nFE°<sub>cell</sub> = 4 × 96500 × 1.23 ≈ 474,780 J ≈ 474.8 kJ. Since electrolysis is the exact thermodynamic reverse of the fuel-cell reaction, by the same magnitude of ΔG° (just opposite sign), splitting the same amount of water back into H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> requires at least this same 474.8 kJ of electrical energy input (in practice, more, due to overpotentials and inefficiencies).
questions.hint: Recall that for a reaction and its exact reverse, |ΔG°| (and hence the theoretical energy involved) is identical; only the sign, and hence whether energy is released or required, flips.
distractor_logic: This gets the correct magnitude for the fuel cell but wrongly assumes electrolysis needs only half as much energy; thermodynamically, reversing a process requires at least as much energy as was released by the forward process.
This uses n = 2 instead of the given n = 4 (halving the correct magnitude) for the fuel cell energy calculation.
ΔG° magnitudes are identical (equal and opposite) for forward and reverse reactions; treating them as unrelated ignores this fundamental thermodynamic symmetry.

questions.question: A student measures Λ<sub>m</sub>° for a weak acid using Kohlrausch's law and separately determines E°<sub>cell</sub> = 0.20 V (n = 2) for a related redox reaction of the same acid's conjugate base. If log K (from E°<sub>cell</sub>) is used to estimate the acid's dissociation constant K<sub>a</sub> is this a valid approach?
options: No; K<sub>a</sub> can only ever be measured using conductivity, never through any other method
Yes; K from any electrochemical measurement always equals K<sub>a</sub> for the same molecule

No; log K derived from E°<sub>cell</sub> corresponds to the equilibrium constant of the specific redox reaction described, not to the acid-dissociation equilibrium constant K<sub>a</sub>, which is a completely different (non-redox, proton-transfer) equilibrium
Yes, but only if n happens to equal 1
questions.explanation: K derived from the Nernst/Gibbs relationship (log K = nE°<sub>cell</sub>/0.0591) is the equilibrium constant specifically for the redox half-reactions that make up that particular cell reaction; K<sub>a</sub> describes an entirely different equilibrium (proton transfer/dissociation, no electron transfer), so the two constants are conceptually and numerically unrelated unless the redox reaction happens to be the dissociation itself (which it is not here).
questions.hint: Ask what equilibrium each K actually describes: K (from E°<sub>cell</sub>) describes a redox reaction; K<sub>a</sub> describes an acid dissociation. Different reactions have different equilibrium constants.
distractor_logic: This statement is too absolute and also doesn't address the actual conceptual mismatch being tested; conductivity is one valid method, but the claim that it is the ONLY possible method is an overstatement, and it still sidesteps why the redox K here is inapplicable.
The value of n does not change the fundamental mismatch between what a redox equilibrium constant and an acid dissociation constant each represent.
K<sub>a</sub> can, in principle, be estimated by several independent methods (conductivity via Kohlrausch's law being one common one in this chapter), not exclusively by conductivity.

questions.question: A cell reaction relies on ion movement through solution (via molar conductivity considerations) as well as electron transfer at the electrodes. If the molar conductivity of the electrolyte in a Daniell cell's salt bridge is very low, what practical effect would this have on the cell's performance, even though E°<sub>cell</sub> itself is unaffected?
options: The cell's E°<sub>cell</sub> value itself would decrease significantly
There would be no effect at all on the cell's practical operation
The cell reaction would become non-spontaneous
The cell would show a higher internal resistance, reducing the maximum current it can deliver, even though the thermodynamic driving force (E°<sub>cell</sub>) remains unchanged
questions.explanation: E°<sub>cell</sub> is a thermodynamic quantity determined by the electrode couples' standard potentials and is unaffected by the salt bridge's conductivity; however, low molar conductivity in the salt bridge means higher internal (ionic) resistance, which limits the rate at which the cell can actually deliver current in practice, even though its theoretical driving force is unchanged.
questions.hint: Separate 'how strong is the push' (E°<sub>cell</sub>, thermodynamics) from 'how easily can charge actually flow' (conductivity, a kinetic/transport property).
distractor_logic: E°<sub>cell</sub> is determined solely by the electrode half-reactions' standard potentials, not by the salt bridge's ionic conductivity.
A poorly conducting salt bridge does have a real practical consequence (limiting achievable current), even though it leaves the thermodynamics untouched.

Spontaneity is governed by the sign of ΔG° (and hence E°<sub>cell</sub>), which is unrelated to how conductive the salt bridge is; a low-conductivity bridge slows the cell down but does not make the reaction thermodynamically unfavourable.
